claim: Local field potential (LFP) recordings reflect the dynamics of the current source density (CSD) in brain tissue.
source: Local field potential (LFP) recordings reflect the dynamics of the current source density (CSD) in brain tissue.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract supported by citations to established literature (Lindén et al., 2011; Buzsáki et al., 2012; Einevoll et al., 2013; Pesaran et al., 2018; Sinha and Narayanan, 2022) in the introduction.

claim: The model simultaneously captured spiking and CSD responses.
source: The model simultaneously captured spiking and CSD responses and demonstrated a two-way dissociation: firing rates are altered with minor effects on the CSD pattern by adjusting synaptic weights, and CSD is altered with minor effects on firing rates by adjusting synaptic placement on the dendrites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study, supported by the experimental and modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Firing rates are altered with minor effects on the CSD pattern by adjusting synaptic weights.
source: The model simultaneously captured spiking and CSD responses and demonstrated a two-way dissociation: firing rates are altered with minor effects on the CSD pattern by adjusting synaptic weights, and CSD is altered with minor effects on firing rates by adjusting synaptic placement on the dendrites.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5 and related text showing that synaptic weight adjustments changed firing rates while CSD patterns remained largely unchanged.

claim: CSD is altered with minor effects on firing rates by adjusting synaptic placement on the dendrites.
source: The model simultaneously captured spiking and CSD responses and demonstrated a two-way dissociation: firing rates are altered with minor effects on the CSD pattern by adjusting synaptic weights, and CSD is altered with minor effects on firing rates by adjusting synaptic placement on the dendrites.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 5F-G showing that changing synaptic placement substantially altered CSD while firing rates remained similar.

claim: Thalamocortical inputs and recurrent connections sculpt specific sinks and sources early in the visual response.
source: We describe how thalamocortical inputs and recurrent connections sculpt specific sinks and sources early in the visual response, whereas cortical feedback crucially alters them in later stages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the analysis in Figure 7 showing contributions of different input sources to CSD patterns at different time periods.

claim: Cortical feedback crucially alters sinks and sources in later stages of the visual response.
source: We describe how thalamocortical inputs and recurrent connections sculpt specific sinks and sources early in the visual response, whereas cortical feedback crucially alters them in later stages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6 showing that adding feedback from higher visual areas was necessary to reproduce the sustained L2/3 sink and L4 source observed experimentally.

claim: The model is comprised of >50,000 biophysically detailed neuron models.
source: The model is comprised of >50,000 biophysically detailed neuron models surrounded by an annulus of almost 180,000 generalized leaky-integrate-and-fire units.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model composition from the abstract, confirmed in the methods section.

claim: The neuron models belong to 17 different cell type classes.
source: The neuron models belong to 17 different cell type classes: one inhibitory class (Htr3a) in layer 1, and four classes in each of the other layers (2/3, 4, 5, and 6) where one is excitatory and three are inhibitory (Pvalb, Sst, Htr3a) in each layer.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model architecture from the abstract.

claim: The visual coding dataset consists of simultaneous recordings from six Neuropixels 1.0 probes across a range of cortical and subcortical structures in 58 mice.
source: The visual coding dataset consists of simultaneous recordings from six Neuropixels 1.0 probes across a range of cortical and subcortical structures in 58 mice while they are exposed to a range of visual stimuli (about 100,000 units and 2 billion spikes over 2 hr of recording).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental dataset from the introduction.

claim: The LFP predominantly stems from currents caused by synaptic inputs and their associated return currents through the membranes.
source: While the high-frequency component of the extracellular potential, the single- or multi-unit activity (MUA), primarily reflects action potentials of one or more nearby neurons, the LFP predominantly stems from currents caused by synaptic inputs (Mitzdorf, 1985; Einevoll et al., 2007) and their associated return currents through the membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to established literature.

claim: The first principal component of the CSD explains 50.4% of the variance across animals.
source: The first principal component (PC 1) (Figure 2B) constitutes a sum of weighted contributions of the CSD patterns from all 44 animals and explains half (50.4%) of the variance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An early transient sink arises in layer 4 approximately 40 ms after flash onset.
source: In the first four animals (#1–4), we observe an early transient sink arising in layer 4 (L4) ~40 ms after flash onset, followed by a sustained source starting ~60 ms, which covers L4 and parts of layers 2/3 (L2/3) and layer 5 (L5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Figure 2A and is visible in the CSD plots.

claim: A sustained source covering L4 and parts of L2/3 and L5 starts around 60 ms after flash onset.
source: In the first four animals (#1–4), we observe an early transient sink arising in layer 4 (L4) ~40 ms after flash onset, followed by a sustained source starting ~60 ms, which covers L4 and parts of layers 2/3 (L2/3) and layer 5 (L5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Figure 2A and is visible in the CSD plots.

claim: A sustained sink covering layers 5 and 6 emerges around 50 ms after flash onset.
source: We also observe a sustained sink covering layers 5 and 6 (L6) emerging around 50 ms, as well as a sustained sink covering layers 1 and 2/3 around 60 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Figure 2A and is visible in the CSD plots.

claim: A sustained sink covering layers 1 and 2/3 emerges around 60 ms after flash onset.
source: We also observe a sustained sink covering layers 5 and 6 (L6) emerging around 50 ms, as well as a sustained sink covering layers 1 and 2/3 around 60 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing Figure 2A and is visible in the CSD plots.

claim: The inter-trial variability in CSD is significantly lower than the inter-animal variability in trial-averaged CSD.
source: By computing the pairwise Wasserstein distances between single trial CSDs within each animal and comparing it to the pairwise WD between the trial-averaged CSD of each animal, we find that inter-trial variability in CSD is significantly lower than the inter-animal variability in trial-averaged CSD (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance = 0.33; p<0.001) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with statistical support and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The majority of animals (39 out of 44) have a Wasserstein distance to PC 1 CSD that is less than half of the greatest WD between individual animals and PC 1 CSD.
source: The majority of animals (39 out of 44) have a WD to the first principal component, PC 1, of the CSD that is less than half of the greatest WD between the CSD of individual animals and the PC 1 CSD (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Fast-spiking neurons have population firing rates more than twice as high as regular-spiking cells during baseline, peak, and sustained periods.
source: The population firing rates for FS neurons are more than twice as high as RS cells during baseline, peak, and sustained.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Among regular-spiking populations, the firing rate in L5 is the highest in all periods.
source: Among the RS populations, the firing rate in L5 is the highest in all periods, followed by L4 and L6, while L2/3 has the lowest firing rates (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The original model's CSD exhibits a strong sink in the L5 and L6 region starting at approximately 50 ms after flash onset.
source: The inferred CSD exhibits a strong sink in the L5 and L6 region, matched by a strong source below it, both starting at ~50 ms after flash onset (Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the original model and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The early L4 sink, the later sustained L4 source, and the sustained L2/3 sink are either absent or too weak in the original model compared to experimental observations.
source: However, the early L4 sink, the later sustained L4 source, and the sustained L2/3 sink typically observed in the experimental CSD (Figure 2A, B) are either absent or too weak compared to the sink and source in L5 and L6.
evidence: This is stated in the results section comparing the original model to experimental data.

claim: The Wasserstein distance from the original model's CSD to the experimental PC 1 CSD is greater than the WD of the farthest outlier animal.
source: The WD from the simulated CSD to the experimental PC 1 CSD is greater than the WD between the CSD of the farthest outlier animal and the PC 1 CSD (WD = 1.84, normalized to the largest WD between CSD of individual animals and PC 1 CSD).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Adjusting recurrent synaptic weights brought model firing rates within experimental variability for all populations.
source: We multiplied the recurrent synaptic weights with factors in the [0.2, 2.5] range until we arrived at a set of weights where none of the model firing rates were among the experimental outliers in any time window (KSSb = 0.73, KSSp = 0.77, and KSSs = 0.70; average across RS populations and the FS population) and temporal profiles (RS L2/3: r = 0.49***, RS L4: r = 0.63***, RS L5: r = 0.71***, RS L6: r = 0.87***, FS: r = 0.86***; *** p<0.001) (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The CSD pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting synaptic weights to match experimental firing rates.
source: The resulting pattern (but not the magnitude) of the CSD, however, was largely unchanged (Figure 5D) compared to the original CSD (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5D compared to Figure 4B.

claim: Placing all excitatory synapses onto basal dendrites of L4 excitatory neurons increased their contribution to the total CSD by a factor of approximately 2.
source: We tested the effects of synaptic location by placing all synapses from both LGN and excitatory neurons onto the basal dendrites of L4 excitatory neurons (within the same ranges as in the original configuration). This increased the contribution from the L4 excitatory neurons to the total CSD (Figure 5F, middle row, leftmost plot) by a factor of ~2
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The firing rate of L4 excitatory cells remained essentially unchanged when all synapses were moved to basal dendrites.
source: The firing rate of the L4 excitatory cells, however, remained essentially unchanged by this modification (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Somatic Hodgkin-Huxley channels significantly shape the CSD pattern.
source: We also find that the somatic Hodgkin–Huxley channels significantly shapes the CSD pattern (Figure 5H), generating a source in the L4 region where the somata are localized.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Feedback from higher visual areas can exert a powerful influence on the magnitude of the evoked LFP response recorded in V1.
source: Hartmann et al., 2019 found that feedback from higher visual areas (HVAs) can exert a powerful influence on the magnitude of the evoked LFP response recorded in V1 of macaque monkeys, particularly in the period 80–100 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to Hartmann et al., 2019.

claim: Synapses from higher visual areas terminate on L1 and L2/3 apical dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: Furthermore, anatomical data indicate that synapses from HVAs terminate on L1 and L2/3 apical dendrites of pyramidal cells (whose cell bodies reside in L2/3 or L5) (Glickfeld and Olsen, 2017; Marques et al., 2018; Hartmann et al., 2019; Keller et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The sustained L2/3 sink and L4 source might be induced by feedback from higher visual areas.
source: Together, these observations suggest that the sustained L2/3 sink and L4 source might, in part, be induced by feedback from HVAs, where the sink is generated from the input to the apical tufts in L1 and L2/3, and the source may be the return currents of this input.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis based on multiple observations.

claim: The feedback from LM to V1 is best characterized among higher visual areas.
source: Of these HVAs, the feedback from LM to V1 is best characterized (Marques et al., 2018; Keller et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020) and has the highest connection density to V1 (Harris et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The public Neuropixels dataset has 2075 neurons recorded in LM from 42 animals during presentations of the full-field flash stimulus.
source: In total, the public Neuropixels dataset has 2075 neurons recorded in LM (simultaneously with the recordings in LGN, V1, and other visual areas) from 42 animals during presentations of the full-field flash stimulus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset from the results section.

claim: When the model received feedback input together with LGN input, the resulting CSD pattern reproduced the main features observed in experiments.
source: When the model received this feedback input together with the LGN input, the resulting CSD pattern reproduced the main features observed in the experiments (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Wasserstein distance between the final model CSD and the experimental PC 1 CSD was no longer an outlier.
source: The WD between the model CSD and the experimental PC 1 CSD was also no longer an outlier (Normalized WD = 0.41; Figure 6D)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The final adjusted model exhibits both CSD and firing rate patterns that are consistent with experimental observations and well within animal variability.
source: Thus, when average responses to the full-field flash are considered, this final adjusted model exhibits both the CSD and firing rate patterns that are consistent with the experimental observations and are well within animal variability (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: The early L4 sink originates in the thalamocortical input to L4 excitatory cells.
source: We found that the initial L4 sink originates in the thalamocortical input to L4 excitatory cells, which aligns with suggestions made in Mitzdorf, 1987, Swadlow et al., 2002, and Senzai et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The sustained L5/L6 sink comes from postsynaptic currents in L6 excitatory cells triggered by a combination of thalamocortical and recurrent excitatory inputs.
source: The sustained L5/L6 sink comes from postsynaptic currents in L6 excitatory cells triggered by a combination of thalamocortical and recurrent excitatory inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The sustained L2/3 sink stems, in part, from input from LM onto the apical tufts of L2/3 and L5 excitatory cells.
source: The sustained L2/3 sink stems, in part, from input from LM onto the apical tufts of L2/3 and L5 excitatory cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The sustained L4 source has its origins in a mixture of return currents from L2/3 and L5 excitatory cells resulting from feedback onto the apical dendrites.
source: The sustained L4 source has its origins in a mixture of return currents from L2/3 and L5 excitatory cells resulting from the abovementioned feedback onto the apical dendrites of these cells, as well as contributions from L4 excitatory and inhibitory cells (Figure 7A, B, D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Somatic voltage-dependent membrane currents significantly shape the CSD signature.
source: In line with observations made by Reimann et al., 2013, we found that the somatic voltage-dependent membrane currents significantly shape the CSD signature (Figures 5H and 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and shown in Figures 5H and 7C.

claim: The addition of synaptic input and changes to synaptic placement substantially altered the CSD pattern.
source: Even so, our findings still emphasize the importance of synaptic inputs in sculpting the CSD, as the addition of synaptic input (Figure 6A–E) and changes to synaptic placement (Figure 5F) substantially altered the CSD pattern.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and shown in Figures 5F and 6A-E.

claim: Inhibitory cells make up about 15% and excitatory cells about 85% of the total number of cells in the V1 model.
source: In this V1 model, inhibitory cells make up about 15% and excitatory cells about 85% of the total number of cells, reflecting the cellular composition in mouse V1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section describing the model composition.

claim: The canonical CSD pattern in response to a full-field flash explains half (50.4%) of the variance in the trial-averaged CSD responses across animals.
source: This canonical CSD, in response to a flashed, bright field pattern, explains half (50.4 %) of the variance in the trial-averaged CSD responses across animals.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section summarizing the findings.

claim: Both the early L4 sink with concurrent sources above and below and the L5/L6 sink with a source below were observed with similar timing by Senzai et al., 2019.
source: Both the early L4 sink with concurrent sources above and below and the L5/L6 sink with a source below were observed with a similar timing by Senzai et al., 2019.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with a citation.

claim: Studies in non-human primates where animals were exposed to flashes demonstrate good spatio-temporal agreement with the CSD observed in this study.
source: Studies in non-human primates where the animals were exposed to flashes also demonstrate good spatio-temporal agreement with the CSD observed here, with sinks and sources occurring not only in the same layers and in the same order, but also at the same time after stimulus presentation (Givre et al., 1994; Schroeder et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: The original model produced firing rates and orientation and direction tuning consistent with recordings in vivo.
source: The original model used as a starting point here produced firing rates and direction and orientation tuning consistent with recordings during presentations of drifting gratings (Arkhipov et al., 2018; Billeh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section with citations.

claim: The revised model continued to exhibit orientation and direction tuning when tested with drifting gratings stimulus.
source: In this study, we focused on the analysis and modeling of the response to full-field flashes, but when the final model was tested with the drifting gratings stimulus utilized in Billeh et al., 2020, we found that the present, revised model continued to exhibit orientation and direction tuning even though the adjustments were made with the aim to reproduce the observed CSD and population firing rates during full-field flashes (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: The model contains 230,924 neurons in total.
source: In total, there are 51,978 multicompartment neurons with Hodgkin–Huxley conductances at the soma and only passive conductances at the dendrites. These are arranged in a cylinder of radius of 400 μm and height 860 μm (corresponding to the average cortical thickness of V1 taken from the Allen CCF; Billeh et al., 2020; Oh et al., 2014). This cylinder makes up the 'core' of the model and is surrounded by an annulus of 178,946 are LIF neurons which has the same height and a thickness of 445 μm. This makes the total number of neurons in the model 230,924
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the model.

claim: The model core has a radius of 400 μm and a height of 860 μm.
source: These are arranged in a cylinder of radius of 400 μm and height 860 μm (corresponding to the average cortical thickness of V1 taken from the Allen CCF; Billeh et al., 2020; Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the model architecture.

claim: The LGN module providing thalamocortical input to the model consists of 17,400 units.
source: The LGN module providing thalamocortical input to the model consists of 17,400 units selectively connected to the excitatory neurons and Pvalb neurons in L2/3 to L6, as well as the non-Pvalb neurons in L1.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the model.

claim: A Poisson source firing at 1 kHz provides background input to all cells representing the influence from the rest of the brain.
source: The background input to all neurons in the model comes from a single Poisson source firing at 1 kHz and represents influence from the rest of the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the model inputs.

claim: Out of 58 animals in the dataset, 44 were retained for CSD analysis.
source: Out of the 58 animals in the dataset, 5 did not have readable recordings of LFP in V1 during the presentation of the full-field flash stimuli, and the exact probe locations in V1 could not be recovered for 9 other animals due to fading of fluorescent dye or artifacts in the optical projection tomography (OPT) volume (see 'Materials and methods'). The remaining 44 (out of the 58) animals in the dataset were retained for the CSD analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the data quality control.

claim: The CSD was calculated from the LFP using the delta iCSD method.
source: The CSD can be estimated from the LFP (averaged over 75 trials) using the delta iCSD method to obtain a more localized measure of inflowing (sinks) and outflowing currents (sources) (Pettersen et al., 2006; Einevoll et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to the method.

claim: Neuropixels probes record LFP and hundreds of units across the cortical depth in multiple areas with 20 μm spacing between recording channels.
source: In particular, the Neuropixels probes (Jun et al., 2017) record LFP and hundreds of units across the cortical depth in multiple areas, with 20 μm spacing between recording channels allowing for an unprecedented level of spatial detail.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: The model is freely accessible to the community.
source: The new model obtained here is freely accessible (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.k3j9kd5b8) to the community to facilitate further applications of biologically detailed modeling.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Spikes and LFP were recorded across multiple brain areas with a focus on six cortical and two thalamic visual areas using Neuropixels probes in 58 mice.
source: Spikes and LFP were recorded across multiple brain areas, with a focus on six cortical (V1, LM, AL, RL, AM, PM) and two thalamic (LGN, LP) visual areas, using Neuropixels probes in 58 mice (Siegle et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation.

claim: The LFP is a more easily and stably recorded signal in chronic settings than spikes.
source: The LFP is also a promising signal for steering neuroprosthetic devices (Mehring et al., 2003; Andersen et al., 2004; Rickert et al., 2005; Markowitz et al., 2011; Stavisky et al., 2015) and for monitoring neural activity in human recordings (Mukamel and Fried, 2012) because the LFP is more easily and stably recorded in chronic settings than spikes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Current sinks and sources are constrained by Kirchoff's current law.
source: The current sinks and sources indicate where positive ions flow into and out of cells, respectively, and are constrained by Kirchoff's current law (i.e., currents sum to zero over the total membrane area of a neuron).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a fundamental principle.

claim: The interpretation of current sinks and sources is inherently ambiguous as several processes can be the origin.
source: However, the interpretation of current sinks and sources is inherently ambiguous as several processes can be the origin of a current sink or source (Buzsáki, 2006; Pettersen et al., 2006; Einevoll et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A current source may reflect an inhibitory synaptic current or an outflowing return current resulting from excitatory synaptic input elsewhere on the neuron.
source: For example, a current source may reflect an inhibitory synaptic current or an outflowing return current resulting from excitatory synaptic input elsewhere on the neuron. There is no simple way of knowing which it is from an extracellular recording alone (Buzsáki, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation, illustrating the ambiguity in interpreting CSD.

claim: Utilizing the LFP and/or the CSD in modeling can aid model configuration and implementation by revealing discrepancies between models and experiments.
source: Our findings demonstrate that utilizing the LFP and/or the CSD in modeling can aid model configuration and implementation by revealing discrepancies between models and experiments and provide additional constraints on model parameters beyond those offered by the spiking activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: CSD analysis provides powerful constraints for modeling beyond those from considering spikes.
source: These results establish quantitative links between macroscopic brain measurements (LFP/CSD) and microscopic biophysics-based understanding of neuron dynamics and show that CSD analysis provides powerful constraints for modeling beyond those from considering spikes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Comparing the simulated CSD to the experimental CSD revealed discrepancies between model and data that were not apparent from only comparing the firing rates.
source: Furthermore, we found that comparing the simulated CSD to the experimental CSD revealed discrepancies between model and data that were not apparent from only comparing the firing rates.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding.

claim: It was not until feedback from higher cortical visual areas was added to the model that simulations reproduced both the experimentally recorded CSD and firing rates.
source: Additionally, it was not until feedback from higher cortical visual areas (HVAs) was added to the model that simulations reproduced both the experimentally recorded CSD and firing rates, as opposed to only the firing rates.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding.
